### Introduction

T20 cricket is a fast-paced format where match situations can change quickly, and individual deliveries can have a significant impact on the result. Each team has a maximum of 20 overs to score runs. This means the batting team must balance scoring quickly with keeping wickets in hand. Playing too cautiously can leave too many runs to score, while being too aggressive can lead to losing wickets and make it harder to score later in the innings. As a result, a player's performance needs to be considered in the context of the match situation.

This is particularly important when a team is chasing a target. The batting team must consider how many runs are needed, how many deliveries remain and how many wickets are available. These factors affect the difficulty of the chase and the decisions players make. Similarly, a bowler's performance depends on the situation in which they bowl. Restricting runs or taking wickets can be more difficult depending on the stage of the innings and the position of the batting team.

Traditional statistics such as batting averages, strike rates and bowling economy rates provide useful measures of player performance. However, they do not fully account for the match situation in which those performances occur. Looking at these statistics alongside match-state information can provide a better understanding of how players perform under different conditions.

This project examines player performance in the Big Bash League (BBL) using historical ball-by-ball data. This data allows each match to be analysed delivery by delivery, taking into account how the match develops over time. The project focuses on two questions: how well match-state and player-related factors can predict the likelihood of a wicket on a given delivery, and which bowlers are most effective at restricting runs and taking wickets during the death overs after accounting for the match situations in which they bowl.

### The overall project consisted of six research questions which were divided among the three members of the group. 
1. How do scoring rates and wicket probabilities vary across the three phases of a T20 innings — the Powerplay (overs 1–6), the middle overs (7–16), and the death overs (17–20)?

2. Can we build a model that predicts the probability of a wicket falling on any given delivery, using match-state and player-identity features?

3. Which batters perform best under high-pressure chase situations — defined by a high required run rate and few wickets in hand — relative to their performance in low-pressure situations?

4. Which bowlers are most effective at restricting runs and taking wickets in the death overs, after controlling for the match state they bowl in?

5. Does winning the toss and choosing to field (the more common decision in T20) actually translate into a meaningful advantage?

6. Do players naturally cluster into distinct batting or bowling archetypes based on their ball-by-ball performance profiles?
